cards.b:
Newton's laws tell a cricket ball where to go. Erwin Schrödinger's equation (Zurich, early 1926) does the same job for the wavefunction of an electron or atom: it tells you how ψ changes in time. From it we can compute the colours of atoms, the shapes of molecules and the behaviour of every chip in your phone.

Schrödinger shared the 1933 Nobel Prize with Paul Dirac.

Schrödinger's equation

The rate at which ψ changes in time depends on the energy of the system (its "Hamiltonian"): iħ ∂ψ/∂t = Hψ. In words: energy decides how the wave evolves.

Like Newton's laws, it is deterministic: given ψ now, it fixes ψ later exactly. The randomness comes only at measurement, when Born's rule gives the odds. Two different rules: smooth evolution between, random jump at a click.

The lowest wave in a box still has some bend in it, so it has energy. A confined particle can never be perfectly at rest. The tighter the box, the higher this minimum energy. That is why atoms do not collapse: squeezing an electron closer to the nucleus raises its energy more than the electric attraction pays back.

This "zero-point energy" is why liquid helium stays liquid even near absolute zero at normal pressure.

Schrödinger solved the hydrogen atom in 1926. His levels matched Bohr's (-13.6 eV divided by n²) but also gave the shapes of the electron clouds (orbitals) and explained why some spectral lines are brighter. Hydrogen has an exact solution; for heavier atoms and molecules, computers give approximate answers. Quantum chemistry and drug design now rely on such computations.

Werner Heisenberg, Max Born and Pascual Jordan had built a different looking theory in 1925, "matrix mechanics", using tables of numbers and no pictures. Schrödinger's waves looked friendlier. In 1926 Schrödinger showed they are mathematically equivalent. Dirac and John von Neumann later put both into one framework.

Honest note: the equation is tested to extraordinary precision, but what ψ represents is the interpretation question.

• Hydrogen spectrum to many decimal places.
  • Molecular spectra, chemistry and bonding.
  • Semiconductors: band structure comes straight from the equation and tells us which materials are chips or insulators.
  • Atomic clocks, which depend on the exact energy levels.

No experiment has contradicted it in its domain (slow, non-relativistic particles). Dirac extended it for speed close to light in 1928.

• "Schrödinger's equation says everything is random." It is perfectly predictable; the dice appear when measuring.
  • "You need heavy maths to grasp it." The idea (waves, fit, energy) is simple; solving it is hard.
  • "It was derived." It cannot be strictly derived from older physics; it was a guess that worked.

cards.h: Raman spectra and Indian quantum chemistry
cards.b: The levels of molecular vibration and rotation come from Schrödinger's equation, and the Raman effect (1928) reads them directly. Raman spectroscopy is used today in Indian labs from IISc and IACS Kolkata (Raman's own institute) to forensic and pharma testing. Quantum chemistry methods, built on this equation, drive materials research under India's National Quantum Mission.

• Schrödinger's equation tells how ψ evolves in time, smoothly and exactly.
  • Confinement gives standing waves, so energy levels and zero-point energy.
  • Randomness enters only with measurement.

Think about it

  1. Why does squeezing an electron into a smaller space raise its energy?
  2. How can a deterministic equation sit with random measurement results?
